doc.title: Michael White interviewed by Monk Rowe, via Zoom, July 10, 2025

chapter: Teaching and spread of New Orleans jazz
title: Advice to young musicians moving to New Orleans
summary: White calls post-Katrina arrivals a double-edged sword, with some playing well but cheap fees hurting local professionals, and generic bebop approaches failing.

story.theme_name: Where jazz stands today: young players, rock, and the audience
story.community_name: Is jazz healthy? Young players, rock and the future

blocks.x: If you had, in your travels if you met a young musician who was really doing well in the music you’re describing, and they want to come to New Orleans and enter the music scene, would you have some specific advice? Well you better – fill in the blank.
That was a set-up I think.

You know there have been, since Hurricane Katrina there has been a generation of musicians, dozens of musicians that have migrated to New Orleans, and they live here and they play. And to me it’s a double edged sword. Some of them are playing very well early style jazz music of all kinds and are very serious about it and are playing on a very high level and I love it. I think it’s great. You know? It’s great to hear that music live. It’s great to have people that take it seriously and respect it you know. But on the other hand from a business perspective and from a New Orleans perspective a lot of musicians are happy to be in New Orleans, happy to play, and some people play let’s just say for low fees. And it makes it harder for professional musicians in New Orleans. A lot of people come here and claim to be New Orleans musicians and they travel all over the world very cheaply and it makes it hard for some of the real New Orleans musicians to go out and you know, under the professional conditions that you should go out under. You know? So it’s kind of like a double edged sword in a way. But it’s very difficult, You know like we were talking about earlier, people go through music schools and different things and they learn how to play, but they don’t really learn about this music so a lot of times the guys that play think oh it’s just a set of chords and I can just play my little bebop style over it

and that works and that’s it. And then they wonder why they don’t get, you know, attention and a career like other people but it’s that generic style, it doesn’t have the same impact as the real New Orleans jazz. I mean it’s a valid style. It’s not about how old it is or how many scales or chords you play over this and that. I mean it’s twelve notes, and I find that I use all the notes and everything but it’s how you use them you know.
